questions.stem: A 71 year old man has 2 months of tiredness, two chest infections treated with antibiotics and bruises on his shins he cannot explain. He has conjunctival pallor and scattered bruises. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which term best describes these blood results?
questions.e: All three cell lines are reduced, which is the definition of pancytopenia.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which term best describes these blood results?
Tiredness (anaemia), infections (low white cells) and bruising (low platelets): one symptom per cell line.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together is pancytopenia.

elim: Agranulocytosis is loss of granulocytes alone; here haemoglobin and platelets are low too.
Platelets are low, but so are haemoglobin and white cells.
That describes immature red and white cells on a film, not a count of three low lines.
True but incomplete: it ignores the low white cells and platelets.

steps.x: E. Pancytopenia. Three low lines on the FBC = pancytopenia; think of a bone marrow problem.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman is 10 days into her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer. She has felt shivery and unwell for 6 hours. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Her chest is clear. Investigations: neutrophils 0.3 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5), platelets 62 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever in a patient with a very low neutrophil count after chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: 10 days into her second cycle of chemotherapy
steps.x: Chemotherapy suppresses the marrow, typically 7 to 14 days after a cycle; neutrophils under 0.5 with fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pancytopenia (or neutropenia) with fever is neutropenic sepsis.

elim: A diagnosis of exclusion; with neutrophils of 0.3 infection must be assumed.
She has not been transfused.
Causes electrolyte and renal problems early after treatment, not fever with tachycardia.
Too benign a label for a febrile, tachycardic neutropenic patient.

steps.x: C. Neutropenic sepsis. Fever plus low neutrophils = neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise; treat as an emergency.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman has 4 months of fatigue and recurrent urinary infections. She had chemotherapy for lymphoma 9 years ago and also has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and knee osteoarthritis. A blood film shows macrocytosis and neutrophils with bilobed, hyposegmented nuclei. Serum B12 and folate are normal. A bone marrow biopsy shows a hypercellular marrow with dysplastic features and ringed sideroblasts.
questions.q: Which feature of her history is the most important risk factor for this condition?
questions.e: Myelodysplastic syndrome is a disease of older people and of those who had chemotherapy or radiotherapy in the past.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which feature of her history is the most important risk factor for this condition?
Pelger-Huët neutrophils and ringed sideroblasts in a hypercellular marrow mean myelodysplastic syndrome.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Name the diagnosis (MDS) then its main risk factors: older age and previous chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

elim: Not a recognised cause of marrow dysplasia.
Irrelevant to haematopoiesis.
A consequence of her neutropenia, not a cause.
Not linked to myelodysplastic syndrome.

steps.x: A. Chemotherapy for lymphoma 9 years ago. Pancytopenia risk factors: older age and previous chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man with epilepsy has 4 weeks of tiredness, gum bleeding and a sore throat. He has taken phenytoin for 3 months. He has pallor and petechiae on his legs. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Blood film shows no abnormal cells and the reticulocyte count is low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A drug such as phenytoin can cause marrow failure: normocytic anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia with no abnormal cells and no organomegaly.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
A recognised drug cause, an empty film and no organomegaly point to a failing, not infiltrated, marrow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pancytopenia after starting phenytoin with a clean film is aplastic anaemia.

elim: The film would usually show circulating myeloid blasts.
Only platelets fall; he has symptoms of all three lines being low.
Mainly older people with macrocytosis and dysplastic neutrophils.
Gives a macrocytic film with hypersegmented neutrophils, not linked to phenytoin.

steps.x: B. Aplastic anaemia. Phenytoin or methotrexate plus pancytopenia with a normal film = aplastic anaemia (marrow failure).

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with prostate cancer diagnosed 3 years ago has 2 months of back pain, fatigue and nosebleeds. His PSA has risen to 210 ng/mL. He has pallor and tenderness over the lumbar spine. A blood film shows nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his pancytopenia?
questions.e: Bony metastases from prostate cancer replace normal marrow, giving pancytopenia with a leukoerythroblastic film.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely cause of his pancytopenia?

clues: nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells
steps.x: Known cancer, rising tumour marker, bone pain and a leukoerythroblastic film mean marrow invasion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Marrow infiltration by metastatic prostate cancer.

elim: Gives an empty film; nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells suggest the marrow is being invaded.
There is no splenomegaly or liver disease.
Possible at his age, but rising PSA and bone pain point to metastases.
Would give macrocytosis and neuropathy, not bone pain and a leukoerythroblastic film.

steps.x: B. Bone marrow infiltration by metastases. Pancytopenia comes from marrow failure or marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, metastasis).

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has 3 weeks of fevers, bleeding gums and breathlessness. She was well before this. Her temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. She has gum hypertrophy and petechiae. Investigations: haemoglobin 76 g/L (115–165), white cell count 2.4 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 18 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the blood film?
questions.e: A rapid onset with gum hypertrophy suggests acute myeloid leukaemia, a rapid accumulation of immature myeloid blasts seen on the film.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely finding on the blood film?
A short history, a previously well adult and gum infiltration are typical of AML.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Diagnosis is AML, so the film shows myeloid blasts.

elim: The film of B12 or folate deficiency, which develops over months.
The Pelger-Huët change of myelodysplastic syndrome, usually in older people.
Typical of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, an indolent disease of older adults.
Seen in hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis, which do not cause pancytopenia.

steps.x: A. Circulating myeloid blasts. AML: rapid onset pancytopenia with immature myeloid blasts on the film.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has 6 months of tiredness, a sore tongue and tingling in both feet. She has vitiligo. She has pallor, a smooth red tongue and reduced vibration sense at the ankles. Blood film shows macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Investigations: haemoglobin 82 g/L (115–165), MCV 118 fL (80–100), white cell count 3.1 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 104 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her pancytopenia?
questions.e: B12 deficiency is a reversible cause of pancytopenia; neuropathy, glossitis, vitiligo and hypersegmented neutrophils point to pernicious anaemia.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely cause of her pancytopenia?
Macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils and neuropathy in a woman with autoimmune disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: B12 deficiency (likely pernicious anaemia) causing pancytopenia.

elim: No blasts, and the history is too long and neurological.
Causes a normocytic anaemia with a normal film.
Can raise the MCV but does not cause pancytopenia with neuropathy.
Also macrocytic, but gives hyposegmented, not hypersegmented, neutrophils.

steps.x: E. Vitamin B12 deficiency. Always think of B12 or folate deficiency as a treatable cause of macrocytic pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has 3 months of weight loss, night sweats and recurrent oral thrush. He has had several male sexual partners without condoms. He has seborrhoeic dermatitis and oral candidiasis. Investigations: haemoglobin 104 g/L (130–180), white cell count 2.6 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 96 ×10⁹/L (150–400). Blood film shows no blasts.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his pancytopenia?
questions.e: Viral infection, particularly HIV, is a recognised cause of pancytopenia; thrush and seborrhoeic dermatitis suggest immunosuppression.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his pancytopenia?

clues: several male sexual partners without condoms
steps.x: Risk exposure plus clinical signs of immunosuppression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HIV causing pancytopenia; test for it.

elim: Does not explain oral candidiasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis and his sexual history.
No dietary or alcohol history, and would not explain the infections.
A disease of older people, often after chemotherapy.
Rarely causes pancytopenia and does not cause oral thrush.

steps.x: C. HIV infection. Remember viral causes (HIV) and drugs/toxins among the other causes of pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has 2 months of fatigue, drenching night sweats and nosebleeds. His temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. Investigations show haemoglobin 88 g/L, white cell count 2.0 ×10⁹/L and platelets 35 ×10⁹/L. His doctor is trying to decide between marrow infiltration and aplastic anaemia.
questions.q: Which examination finding most strongly suggests marrow infiltration?
questions.e: Lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly suggest lymphoma or leukaemia infiltrating the marrow; aplastic anaemia has no organomegaly.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which examination finding most strongly suggests marrow infiltration?
Pallor, bruising and fever come from the low counts; only organomegaly points to the cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Look for lymph nodes and spleen: they point to infiltration (lymphoma, leukaemia).

elim: Found in any cause of anaemia.
Found with infection in any neutropenic patient.
Found with any cause of thrombocytopenia.
Reflects anaemia or fever, not the cause.

steps.x: E. Splenomegaly with lymphadenopathy. Examine for pallor, bruising, fever, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly; the last two suggest infiltration.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with pancytopenia from myelodysplastic syndrome is reviewed in clinic. She describes breathlessness on stairs, two chest infections this winter, fatigue, pallor noticed by her daughter and recurrent nosebleeds. Investigations: haemoglobin 91 g/L (115–165), neutrophils 1.1 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5), platelets 22 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which of her symptoms is most directly explained by her low platelet count?
questions.e: Thrombocytopenia causes bleeding: easy bruising and nosebleeds. Anaemia gives fatigue and pallor; neutropenia gives infections.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which of her symptoms is most directly explained by her low platelet count?
Match each symptom to a cell line.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bleeding goes with platelets.

elim: Due to anaemia.
Due to anaemia.
Due to anaemia.
Due to neutropenia.

steps.x: E. Recurrent nosebleeds. Anaemia = fatigue; neutropenia = infections; thrombocytopenia = bruising and nosebleeds.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has 5 months of fatigue and slow-healing leg cuts. He is pale. Investigations: haemoglobin 94 g/L (130–180), MCV 108 fL (80–100), white cell count 2.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 88 ×10⁹/L (150–400), serum B12 and folate normal, TSH normal. He drinks no alcohol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his blood film?
questions.e: An elderly man with macrocytic pancytopenia and normal B12, folate, TSH and no alcohol most likely has myelodysplastic syndrome, which shows the Pelger-Huët anomaly.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely finding on his blood film?
Common causes of macrocytosis have been excluded in an older man.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: MDS, so the film shows Pelger-Huët (hyposegmented, bilobed) neutrophils.

elim: Seen in acute myeloid leukaemia, which presents over weeks.
Seen in B12 or folate deficiency, excluded by normal levels.
Fragmented cells of microangiopathic haemolysis.
Seen in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, with a high lymphocyte count.

steps.x: C. Hyposegmented bilobed neutrophils. MDS: macrocytic anaemia with Pelger-Huët neutrophils.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman sees her GP with 6 weeks of tiredness, gum bleeding and a sore throat that will not settle. She takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 37.4°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. She has pallor and a few petechiae. A full blood count shows haemoglobin 89 g/L, white cell count 1.9 ×10⁹/L and platelets 38 ×10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: After an FBC shows pancytopenia, a blood film looks for abnormal cells (blasts, dysplasia, leukoerythroblastic change) before marrow biopsy.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
The FBC already shows all three lines are low, so the next first-line step is the film.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Look at the cells: blood film.

elim: The gold standard, but it follows the film and is done by haematology.
Used to stage lymphoma or find metastases once a cause is suspected.
Tests for autoimmune haemolysis, not pancytopenia.
Assesses iron stores; iron deficiency does not lower all three lines.

steps.x: A. Blood film. First-line: FBC then blood film; gold standard: bone marrow biopsy.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has 3 months of fatigue and bruising. Investigations show haemoglobin 92 g/L, white cell count 2.3 ×10⁹/L, platelets 45 ×10⁹/L and MCV 102 fL. B12 and folate are normal. The blood film shows no blasts. The haematologist must decide between aplastic anaemia and myelodysplastic syndrome.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Bone marrow biopsy is the gold standard: aplastic anaemia gives a hypocellular, fatty marrow; MDS a hypercellular, dysplastic one.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
Both cause pancytopenia; only the marrow shows whether it is empty or crowded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Look at the marrow directly.

elim: May show splenomegaly but cannot show marrow cellularity.
Already done and non-diagnostic.
Low in both conditions.
Does not separate marrow failure from dysplasia.

steps.x: B. Bone marrow biopsy. Bone marrow biopsy confirms the cause of pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with acute myeloid leukaemia is 9 days after induction chemotherapy. He has had rigors for 1 hour. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. A cannula has been inserted and bloods sent for full blood count.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation before antibiotics are given?
questions.e: Suspected neutropenic sepsis needs blood cultures and then IV antibiotics within an hour (NICE).

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation before antibiotics are given?
Fever after chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cultures, then broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately.

elim: Not relevant to his acute illness.
Useful later if chest signs; must not delay antibiotics.
Dangerous with low platelets and no meningism.
Too narrow; blood cultures are essential in neutropenic sepsis.

steps.x: A. Blood cultures. Neutropenic sepsis: blood cultures then IV antibiotics without delay.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman with psoriatic arthritis is starting weekly methotrexate 15 mg. She is otherwise well and takes no other medicines. Her baseline full blood count, renal function and liver function are normal. Her rheumatologist wants to detect marrow suppression early.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate monitoring investigation?
questions.e: Patients on methotrexate have regular FBCs to detect anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia, with folic acid co-prescribed.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate monitoring investigation?
Monitoring for falling counts in all three lines.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FBC.

elim: Invasive and not used for routine monitoring.
A baseline for lung toxicity, not for marrow suppression.
Does not show whether counts are falling.
Does not assess the marrow.

steps.x: C. Full blood count. Methotrexate: co-prescribe folic acid and monitor the FBC for marrow suppression.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has 4 months of fatigue and breathlessness. He eats a poor diet and drinks 30 units of alcohol a week. Investigations: haemoglobin 84 g/L (130–180), MCV 114 fL (80–100), white cell count 3.0 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 97 ×10⁹/L (150–400). The blood film shows oval macrocytes and no blasts.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Macrocytic pancytopenia in a man with poor diet and alcohol excess needs B12 and folate levels to find a treatable cause.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
Diet and alcohol suggest folate deficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Check B12 and folate.

elim: Reversible causes should be excluded first.
No features of malignancy.
Not relevant to macrocytic pancytopenia.
Iron deficiency gives a low MCV.

steps.x: D. Serum B12 and folate. Before marrow biopsy, exclude B12 and folate deficiency in macrocytic pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has 6 weeks of fatigue, heavy periods and bruising. Investigations: haemoglobin 78 g/L (115–165), MCV 94 fL (80–100), neutrophils 0.6 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5), platelets 14 ×10⁹/L (150–400), reticulocytes low. The blood film shows no abnormal cells. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. A bone marrow biopsy is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on bone marrow biopsy?
questions.e: Normocytic pancytopenia with low reticulocytes, a clean film and no organomegaly in a young adult is aplastic anaemia: a hypocellular, fat-replaced marrow.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely finding on bone marrow biopsy?
A normocytic, empty film picture points to marrow failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Aplastic anaemia, so an empty fatty marrow.

elim: The marrow of myelodysplastic syndrome in an older patient.
No known cancer and no leukoerythroblastic film.
AML; blasts would usually be seen on the film.
Seen in B12 or folate deficiency with macrocytosis.

steps.x: B. Hypocellular marrow replaced by fat. Aplastic anaemia = hypocellular marrow; MDS and leukaemia = hypercellular marrow.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has severe aplastic anaemia confirmed on bone marrow biopsy. No drug or viral cause is found. He has heart failure and chronic kidney disease and is not fit for transplant. He needs red cell transfusions every 3 weeks. His haematologist follows British Society for Haematology guidance.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Aplastic anaemia is treated with immunosuppression or bone marrow transplant; immunosuppression is used when transplant is not suitable.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
Transplant is excluded, which leaves immunosuppression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Immunosuppression (ATG plus ciclosporin).

elim: Curative but he is not fit for it.
Used to lower counts in myeloproliferative disease.
Does not treat marrow failure and transfusions already overload iron.
Used for B cell lymphoma and immune thrombocytopenia, not aplastic anaemia.

steps.x: B. Antithymocyte globulin with ciclosporin. Aplastic anaemia: transplant if fit, otherwise immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with myelodysplastic syndrome has 1 week of worsening breathlessness and dizziness on standing. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Investigations: haemoglobin 58 g/L (115–165), neutrophils 1.4 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5), platelets 41 ×10⁹/L (150–400). She has no bleeding.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.e: Supportive care in pancytopenia: red cells for symptomatic anaemia, platelets for bleeding or very low counts, antibiotics for infection.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
Symptomatic severe anaemia is the urgent problem.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Transfuse red cells.

elim: She is afebrile; neutropenic sepsis is not present.
Too slow and not the cause of her anaemia.
Platelets of 41 without bleeding do not need transfusion.
May reduce long-term transfusion need but too slow for symptomatic Hb 58.

steps.x: D. Red cell transfusion. Treat the cause, and support each line: red cells, platelets, infection control.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with aplastic anaemia awaiting treatment has had a nosebleed for 2 hours despite pressure and nasal packing. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (130–180), neutrophils 0.9 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5), platelets 6 ×10⁹/L (150–400). He is afebrile.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.e: Active bleeding with platelets of 6 needs platelet transfusion as supportive care.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
Bleeding from a very low platelet count.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Give platelets.

elim: Replaces clotting factors; his problem is a lack of platelets.
An adjunct but does not replace missing platelets.
Treats immune thrombocytopenia, not marrow failure.
His haemoglobin is 96 and he is stable.

steps.x: D. Platelet transfusion. Low platelets with bleeding: platelet transfusion.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman presents with 3 weeks of fevers and bleeding gums. Her blood film shows numerous myeloid blasts and bone marrow biopsy shows 60% myeloid blasts. She has been given red cells and platelets, and her fever has settled on IV antibiotics. She is otherwise fit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Pancytopenia is managed by treating the cause; acute myeloid leukaemia is treated with chemotherapy.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
Supportive care is done; she needs treatment of the leukaemia itself.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chemotherapy.

elim: Immunosuppression is for aplastic anaemia.
Treats B12 deficiency.
Treats folate deficiency.
No role in acute leukaemia.

steps.x: B. Intensive chemotherapy. Leukaemia causing pancytopenia: chemotherapy; supportive care alongside.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has pancytopenia with an MCV of 121 fL. She has glossitis and numb feet. Her blood film shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum B12 is 62 ng/L (180–900) and folate is normal. Intrinsic factor antibodies are positive. She has no bleeding and is afebrile.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Pernicious anaemia causing pancytopenia is treated with B12 replacement; counts recover once B12 is replaced.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
B12 deficiency from pernicious anaemia is the cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Replace B12 by injection.

elim: For aplastic anaemia, not a deficiency state.
Not needed for a reversible deficiency.
Folate is normal and folic acid alone can worsen B12 neuropathy.
She is not bleeding and the cause is treatable.

steps.x: C. Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin. B12 deficiency pancytopenia: B12 replacement.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with epilepsy has pancytopenia 2 months after starting phenytoin. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 88 bpm. Blood film shows no abnormal cells and a bone marrow biopsy shows a hypocellular marrow. His haemoglobin is 104 g/L and platelets 48 ×10⁹/L with no bleeding.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop phenytoin and change to another antiepileptic
questions.e: First identify and treat the cause: stop the drug causing marrow failure, with supportive care as needed.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Drug-induced aplastic anaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Remove the drug.

elim: Considered for severe disease not recovering, not before removing the cause.
Leaves the toxic cause in place.
Not a treatment for aplastic anaemia.
No role.

steps.x: E. Stop phenytoin and change to another antiepileptic. Pancytopenia: identify and treat the underlying cause first.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has pancytopenia. His blood film shows macrocytes and hyposegmented neutrophils. A bone marrow biopsy shows a hypercellular marrow with dysplastic features in all lines and ringed sideroblasts. His registrar asks why the blood counts are low when the marrow is full of cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Autoimmune destruction of haematopoietic stem cells
Increased destruction of cells in the spleen
Ineffective dysplastic maturation with cell death within the marrow
questions.e: In MDS, clonal stem cell abnormalities cause dysplastic, ineffective maturation and intramedullary cell death, so peripheral counts stay low despite a busy marrow.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism?

clues: why the blood counts are low
steps.x: A full marrow but empty blood means cells die before release.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ineffective haematopoiesis.

elim: The mechanism of aplastic anaemia, which gives an empty marrow.
Hypersplenism, with no dysplasia.
Myelofibrosis, which gives a dry tap, not a hypercellular dysplastic marrow.
Lowers red cells only.

steps.x: C. Ineffective dysplastic maturation with cell death within the marrow. MDS: hypercellular marrow, low counts from ineffective (dysplastic) maturation.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has 2 weeks of bruising, fatigue and bone pain. Investigations: haemoglobin 81 g/L (130–180), white cell count 1.8 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 22 ×10⁹/L (150–400). Bone marrow biopsy shows a marrow packed with lymphoblasts and almost no normal precursors. He is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pancytopenia?
o: Impaired DNA synthesis from folate deficiency
Malignant blasts crowding out normal haematopoiesis
Pooling of cells in an enlarged spleen
T cell destruction of stem cells
questions.e: In leukaemia, uncontrolled malignant blast proliferation replaces the marrow and crowds out normal haematopoiesis.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pancytopenia?
The marrow is full, but of malignant cells.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Marrow infiltration by blasts.

elim: Immune destruction happens peripherally with an active marrow of normal cells.
Gives megaloblastic change, not a marrow full of blasts.
Hypersplenism, not marrow replacement.
The mechanism of aplastic anaemia, with an empty marrow.

steps.x: C. Malignant blasts crowding out normal haematopoiesis. Leukaemia: hypercellular marrow, normal haematopoiesis crowded out.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes weekly methotrexate. She was given trimethoprim for a urinary infection 10 days ago. She now has mouth ulcers, bruising and a sore throat. Investigations: haemoglobin 92 g/L (115–165), neutrophils 0.7 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5), platelets 48 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her marrow suppression?
o: Blocked tetrahydrofolate synthesis for DNA synthesis
questions.e: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking tetrahydrofolate needed for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing precursors; trimethoprim adds to the antifolate effect.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her marrow suppression?
Two antifolate drugs together.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dihydrofolate reductase inhibition stops DNA synthesis in marrow precursors.

elim: Would lower platelets only.
Urinary infections do not cause this.
Would not lower white cells and platelets.
No features of malignancy; the timing fits the drugs.

steps.x: C. Blocked tetrahydrofolate synthesis for DNA synthesis. Methotrexate = DHFR inhibitor; folic acid reduces toxicity; avoid trimethoprim.
